lines.text: Right, Tom, we've met four people now. We really need to choose someone this week.
I know. Well, I liked the guy who plays the cello. He seemed really relaxed.
Hmm, the cello player. He's nice, but the room he'd get is next to mine, and he practises every evening.
Fair enough. What about the woman we met on Tuesday? The one who works at the hospital?
Priya? Yes, I liked her a lot. She's the person I'd choose, I think. She's tidy and she's quiet.
But she works nights, doesn't she? So she'd be sleeping when we're, er, cooking and watching TV.
That's true. OK, so who's left? The student who brought the cake?
Ha, yes. The cake was amazing. But, um, he asked three times if he could have parties.
No parties. That's the one rule that I'm not going to change. So, not him.
And the last one was Marco, the guy we found through your colleague.
Marco, yes. The man my colleague recommended. She says he's very reliable and he always pays on time.
Did you notice the books that he had in his bag? Cookery books. I mean, a flatmate who cooks? Perfect.
OK, I'm laughing, but you're right. That's important. And he asked questions that were, you know, sensible. About bills and cleaning.
So it's between Priya and Marco, then.
I think so. Shall we invite them both for coffee on Saturday, and decide after that?

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome back to Work Talk. Today's topic is pet peeves at work. Our first caller is Daniel. Daniel, what drives you crazy?

Well, I just put up with it, really. My colleague is a lovely person, very considerate in other ways, so I don't want to upset her.
That's very kind of you. Do you ever say anything?

Ha! Thanks, Daniel. Next on the line is Rosa. Rosa, good morning.

lines.text: Welcome back to Spare Time, the podcast for people who don't have any. I'm Jess.
And I'm Owen. Today we're asking: is having a hobby still possible when you work fifty hours a week?
I think so. For me, running is the answer. Running before work takes thirty minutes, and it clears my head.
See, I tried that. Getting up at six was the problem. I just, er, couldn't do it.
Fair enough. So what did you take up instead?
Knitting. Honestly. Knitting on the train is now my favourite part of the day.
Knitting! I love that. And are you making progress?
Slowly. My first scarf was, um, more of a long square. But finishing something with my own hands feels great.
That's the thing, isn't it? Doing something creative is completely different from doing your job.
Exactly. At work, I stare at a screen. Knitting gives me a break from all that.
Our listeners have sent ideas too. Maya says learning the ukulele is perfect, because practising ten minutes a day is enough.
Ten minutes? I can do that. What else?
Ben says he gave up playing video games and started gardening. He says growing his own tomatoes is worth every minute.
I like that. Although, er, waiting three months for a tomato sounds a bit time-consuming.
Ha! Maybe. So, here's the main message today. Choosing something small is better than doing nothing.

lines.text: Hello, Mr Hughes? It's Clara from number twelve. Sorry to call so late. Have you got a minute?

Would you mind watering my plants while I'm away? Just twice a week. There are quite a lot of them, I'm afraid.

4.title: The Alarm That Didn't Go Off

lines.text: So, this is the story of my first day at my new job. Let me tell you, it wasn't a good start.
The night before, I had set my alarm for six thirty. Or, well, I thought I had.
When I woke up, the sun was shining and it was already eight fifteen.
I realised immediately what had happened. I had set the alarm for six thirty in the evening, not the morning. So it went off at dinner time, and I didn't notice.
Anyway, I got dressed in about three minutes and ran to the station. Of course, there was a delay. A train had broken down further up the line.
Meanwhile, I was sending messages to my new boss. I wrote something like, "So sorry, there's a problem with the trains, I'll be there soon."
By the time I got to the office, it was almost ten. The welcome meeting had already started. Twenty people turned and looked at me.
I wanted to disappear.
But here's the worst part. In the lift, I looked down and realised I had put on two different shoes. One black, one brown.
I hadn't noticed them at home because I'd dressed in the dark. I'd been in such a hurry, you know?
So I walked into the meeting and tried to sit very still behind the table. In the meantime, my boss was talking about, er, the importance of being professional.
Eventually, a woman from the marketing team interrupted me at lunch and said, "Nice shoes." I just laughed. What else could I do?
Later, my boss looked into the train problem and saw that it was true, so she wasn't angry.
And now, two years later, that woman is my best friend at work. She still calls me "Mr Odd Shoes".

5.title: Dinner with a Georgian Family

lines.text: My guest today is Luis, who spent a year teaching English in Georgia. Luis, what's the thing that surprised you most?
Oh, definitely the dinners. The first dinner that I went to lasted, um, five hours.
Five hours! What happens during all that time?
Well, there's a person who leads the whole dinner. He's called the tamada. He's the man who gives all the toasts.
So the tamada is like a host?
Sort of. He's the person everybody listens to. He decides when you drink and what you drink to.
What kind of things do you drink to?
Everything. The country, the family, the people who have died, the children who will be born. Each toast is a little speech.
And did you have to give a toast yourself?
Yes. The thing I was most nervous about was my first toast. I said something about friendship, in very bad Georgian.
How did it go?
Everyone clapped. The family I was living with were really proud of me, I think.
And the food?
Amazing. The dish that everyone knows is khachapuri, bread with cheese and an egg in the middle. But the food that I miss most is a walnut sauce they put on vegetables.
Is there anything you would tell a visitor?
Yes. Be careful with the glass that the tamada fills for you. In some families, you're expected to finish it in one go.
Good advice. Thanks, Luis.

lines.text: My guest is Valeria, a volunteer with a coral project on the island of San Andrés. Valeria, what exactly do you do?
Well, we grow small pieces of coral in underwater nurseries, and then we plant them on the reef in order to help it recover.
Why does the reef need help?
Mainly due to warmer water. When the sea gets too hot, the coral turns white and can die. Pollution affects it too, and so do boats.
And how do you plant coral? It sounds, um, difficult.
It's slow work. We dive twice a day to check the nurseries. Then we use a special glue to fix each piece to the rock.
Is it working?
It is. Thanks to the project, about four thousand pieces have been planted. Every six months, the reef is assessed by scientists to see how many have survived.
And how many have?
About seventy per cent, which is very good. The effect on fish is amazing. We're seeing species that hadn't been here for years.
What's the hardest part of the job?
Honestly? Getting up at five. We go early so as to avoid the strong currents in the afternoon.
And what can tourists do to help?
Simple things. Use reef-safe sun cream, and don't touch the coral. Even one touch can damage it. Some hotels now give guests information to make them aware of this.
Is the work finished?
No, it's ongoing. Climate change has serious consequences, so we'll need to keep planting for years.

14.title: Second Life for Old Phones
14.topic: Describing a process, and adding information precisely

lines.text: My guest today is Carmen Díaz, whose company repairs old phones and sells them again. Carmen, how did it start?
It started in my garage, actually. My brother, who was a student then, kept breaking his phone, so I learned to fix it.
And now you have a factory?
Well, a workshop. We have thirty people, most of whom were trained by us.
So, what happens when a phone arrives?
The phones, which come in batches of about five hundred, are first sorted into three groups. Phones that work, phones that can be repaired, and phones that can't.
And the ones that can't be repaired?
Those are taken apart. The parts that still work are used in other phones. The rest is disposed of safely, by a company that recycles metals.
What's the most common problem?
Batteries, definitely. And cracked screens. A phone whose battery is old feels slow, but often there's nothing else wrong with it.
How do customers know the phones are good?
Every phone goes through quality control. There are, um, about forty checks. Then each one is labelled with a grade, A, B or C, which tells you how it looks.
And who buys them?
Lots of students. And parents who want a cheap first phone for their kids. Our phones are about half the price of new ones.
What problems have you had?
Oh, at the start, everything was a mess. We had to sort out how to track thousands of phones. Now each phone has a code that we scan at every stage.
Carmen, thank you.

lines.text: My guest today is Kemi Adeyemi, who is in the final of the National Young Chef competition next week. Kemi, congratulations.
Thank you! I still can't believe it, to be honest.
Tell us how you started.
Well, I started cooking with my grandmother when I was eight. Then, at sixteen, I opened a small street-food stall at the weekend market.
And how has the stall done?
Really well. We've sold over twenty thousand plates of jollof rice so far. And last year we won the market's best stall prize.
Impressive. When did you enter the competition?
In January. I didn't think I would get far. But I qualified for the semi-final in March, and then, um, somehow I won it.
What has been the biggest accomplishment for you?
Honestly? Cooking for the judges without crying. In the first round, I burned my sauce and had to start again. But I finished on time.
What's the hardest thing you've done in the competition?
The pastry round. I've never been good at pastry. I've practised it every evening for two months now.
Have you had any help?
Yes, my old teacher has been amazing. She's tasted everything I've made. And my mum has come to every round.
And when you look back on the last year, what do you feel?
Proud. I've learned so much. A year ago I'd never cooked for more than ten people. Now I've cooked for hundreds.
Good luck in the final, Kemi.
